newsitem.title: USA: Pound jumps on expectations of higher U.K. interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Pound jumps on expectations of higher U.K. interest rates.

text.p: The British pound rose sharply against the dollar on Friday and hit a five-year high against the German mark amid mounting speculation of higher British interest rates.
At the same time, the dollar rose quietly against the mark and the Japanese yen, although the pound's advance dominated trade.
The pound surpassed 2.86 marks, touching its highest level since August 1992, the start of a run on sterling that drove it out of Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism the following month.
"Sterling has been moving up quite nicely," said Frank Pusateri, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Mellon Bank in Boston.
"Perhaps some fund managers are moving into it in anticipation of a rate hike, so there are some underlying investments moving that," he added.
Against the dollar, the pound rose to $1.6565 from $1.6485.

Britain's new-Labour Party government inherited a robust economy and raised interest rates immediately after defeating the Conservative Party in May. The market believes Labour will deliver more rate hikes to catch up after months of foot-dragging by the previous government.

Investors have been drawn to Britain because of attractive sterling yields and as a haven from uncertainty over Europe's plan to merge currencies in 1999. Britain has not agreed to participate in the new single currency, the euro.
The mark's weakness against the pound indirectly helped lift the dollar against the German currency.

The dollar also rose against the yen, extending a three-day rally as friction over Japan's huge trade surplus ebbed while leaders of the Group of Seven industrial nations gathered for a weekend summit in Denver.
The dollar ended at 1.7275 marks, up from 1.7235 and at 114.88 yen, up from 114.03.
"People are starting to feel a little bit more comfortable on the whole trade issue with Japan," said David Solin, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics, a Connecticut consulting firm.

President Bill Clinton, meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto Thursday evening in Denver, was reported to have voiced concern about Japan's surplus, pointing to the damage to bilateral relations from surpluses in the past.
But Washington is discouraging dollar weakness, even though that might entice Japan to accept more U.S. exports.

Instead, the administration is coaxing Japan to promote domestic-led, rather than export-led growth, and said Thursday that Japan agreed to a formal consultative process to discuss deregulation of its economy.

"The way the U.S. is going to view that is as a kind of step in the right direction," Solin said. "If they feel Japan is moving in the right direction they don't want to come out and continue to bash them on trade."
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka agreed on Friday that excess currency movements were undesirable, a Treasury spokesman said.
In other trading, the dollar was at 1.4385 Swiss francs, up a touch from 1.4380, and at Canadian $1.3910 up from C$1.3878.
